citations.quote:
Let $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ be a real random field in the sense of
[[def-random-field-stationarity-covariance-and-variogram]], and suppose the
finite vector of field values considered below is square-integrable. Choose
$n\ge1$ observation sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ and a target site $s_0$. Write
$Z=(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))^\top$, $Y=X(s_0)$,
$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Z)$, $c_0=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)$, and
$v_0=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. A positive-definite matrix $\Sigma$ means
$u^\top\Sigma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$.

If the mean vector $m=\mathbb E Z$ and target mean $m_0=\mathbb E Y$ are
known, a **simple-kriging linear predictor** with weight vector
$\lambda\in\mathbb R^n$ is
$$\widehat Y_{\mathrm{SK}}(\lambda)=m_0+\lambda^\top(Z-m).$$
Its mean-square prediction error is
$\mathbb E[(Y-\widehat Y_{\mathrm{SK}}(\lambda))^2]$.

For an **ordinary-kriging model**, the mean is an unknown common constant
$\theta$: $\mathbb E Z=\theta\mathbf 1_n$ and $\mathbb E Y=\theta$.
The predictor is $\widehat Y_{\mathrm{OK}}(\lambda)=\lambda^\top Z$.
The admissible ordinary weights satisfy $\mathbf 1_n^\top\lambda=1$.

For a **universal-kriging model**, fix a trend map
$p:T\to\mathbb R^q$, where $q\ge1$, and an unrestricted coefficient vector
$\beta\in\mathbb R^q$. Define the finite-site design matrix
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$ by row $i$ equal to $p(s_i)^\top$, and put
$p_0=p(s_0)$. The model means are $\mathbb E Z=P\beta$ and
$\mathbb E Y=p_0^\top\beta$. The predictor is
$\widehat Y_{\mathrm{UK}}(\lambda)=\lambda^\top Z$; its unbiasedness for
every $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ is expressed by $P^\top\lambda=p_0$.
Ordinary kriging is the special case $q=1$, $P=\mathbf 1_n$, and $p_0=1$.

The covariance-based optimality statements on this page use the actual
finite covariance matrix and vector. In particular, the inverse formula for
simple kriging is not asserted when $\Sigma$ is singular.

finite vector of field values considered below is square-integrable. Choose

Ordinary kriging is the special case $q=1$, $P=\mathbf 1_n$, and $p_0=1$.

The covariance-based optimality statements on this page use the actual
finite covariance matrix and vector. In particular, the inverse formula for
simple kriging is not asserted when $\Sigma$ is singular.

Let $X,Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space, and write
$$W:=\operatorname{span}\big([1],[Y_1],\dots,[Y_n]\big)\subseteq L^2(\mathbb P),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the almost-everywhere class from
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

Then there is a unique class $[Z_*]\in W$ minimizing $\|[X]-[Z]\|_2$ over
$[Z]\in W$. This minimizing class has an affine representative
$Z_*=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n a_jY_j$, and its coefficients satisfy
$$a_0=\mathbb E[X]-\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\mathbb E[Y_j],$$
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)a_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y_i)\qquad(1\le i\le n).$$

The class $[Z_*]$ is unique. If the covariance matrix
$\Gamma=(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j))_{i,j}$ is singular, the coefficient vector
need not be uniquely determined by the normal equations, but any two solutions
yield the same predictor almost surely.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

derivations.claim: For a centered error vector $\varepsilon=Z-\mathbb E Z$ and centered target error $\varepsilon_0=Y-\mathbb E Y$, every unbiased linear predictor has error $\varepsilon_0-\lambda^\top\varepsilon$. Expanding its squared expectation by [F4] gives the common objective $Q(\lambda)=v_0-2\lambda^\top c_0+\lambda^\top\Sigma\lambda$. The centered predictor in the simple case has this same error expression.

In the trend model, $\mathbb E[\lambda^\top Z-Y]=(P^\top\lambda-p_0)^\top\beta$. This expression is zero for every $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ if $P^\top\lambda=p_0$. Conversely, if it is zero for every $\beta$, taking $\beta$ successively to be each coordinate vector shows every coordinate of $P^\top\lambda-p_0$ is zero. Thus the unbiased weights are exactly the affine constraint $P^\top\lambda=p_0$.

Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}$ and suppose $M\binom{x}{y}=0$. The lower block gives $P^\top x=0$. Taking the inner product of $x$ with the upper block gives $x^\top\Sigma x+x^\top Py=0$; the second term is $(P^\top x)^\top y=0$, so positive definiteness gives $x=0$. The upper block now gives $Py=0$, and full column rank gives $y=0$. Hence the finite square matrix $M$ is injective and therefore invertible.

In the simple case, [F3] gives the covariance normal equations $\Sigma\lambda=c_0$ for the minimizing centered affine predictor. Positive definiteness makes the solution unique, $\lambda=\Sigma^{-1}c_0$; substituting it into step 1.1 gives $Q(\lambda)=v_0-c_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}c_0$.

Invertibility gives a unique solution $(\lambda,\nu)$ of the displayed augmented system, and its lower block makes $\lambda$ feasible. For any other feasible vector $\lambda+h$, one has $P^\top h=0$. Using the upper block $\Sigma\lambda+P\nu=c_0$ in the quadratic from step 1.1 gives $Q(\lambda+h)-Q(\lambda)=2h^\top(\Sigma\lambda-c_0)+h^\top\Sigma h=h^\top\Sigma h$. This is positive for nonzero $h$ and zero for $h=0$, so $\lambda$ is the unique constrained minimizer.

Multiplying $\Sigma\lambda+P
u=c_0$ on the left by $\lambda^	op$ and using $P^	op\lambda=p_0$ yields $\lambda^	op\Sigma\lambda+
u^	op p_0=\lambda^	op c_0$. Substitution in $Q(\lambda)$ from step 1.1 gives $Q(\lambda)=v_0-\lambda^	op c_0-
u^	op p_0$, as claimed.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Use the notation of [[def-simple-ordinary-and-universal-kriging]]. For
simple kriging, if $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the unique mean-square
minimizing weight vector is $\lambda_{\mathrm{SK}}=\Sigma^{-1}c_0$, and its
mean-square prediction error is
$$v_0-c_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}c_0.$$

For an unknown trend with design matrix $P$ and target vector $p_0$,
$\lambda^\top Z$ is unbiased for every $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ if and only if
$P^\top\lambda=p_0$. Suppose $\Sigma$ is positive definite and $P$ has full
column rank (that is, $Py=0$ implies $y=0$ for $y\in\mathbb R^q$). Then the
unique unbiased mean-square minimizing weights $\lambda\in\mathbb R^n$ and Lagrange
multiplier $\nu\in\mathbb R^q$ solve
$$\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\nu\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_0\\p_0\end{pmatrix}.$$
The augmented matrix is invertible under these hypotheses. The resulting
mean-square prediction error is
$$v_0-\lambda^\top c_0-\nu^\top p_0.$$
For ordinary kriging, take $P=\mathbf 1_n$ and $p_0=1$, giving
$$\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&\mathbf 1_n\\\mathbf 1_n^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\nu\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Assume AC for existence. For real $X\in L^1(P)$, if $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=X$. If $P(\{X\in B\}\cap A)=P(X\in B)P(A)$ for every real Borel $B$ and $A\in\mathcal G$, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=EX$ almost surely.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

derivations.claim: Let $\lambda=\Sigma^{-1}c_0$ and $R=Y-m_0-\lambda^\top(Z-m)$. By [F1], $(R,Z)$ is jointly Gaussian because each of its linear combinations is a linear combination of $(Y,Z)$. Its residual mean is zero, and $\operatorname{Cov}(R,Z)=c_0^\top-\lambda^\top\Sigma=0$ by the equation $\Sigma\lambda=c_0$.
Applying [F2] to the jointly Gaussian blocks $R$ and $Z$ from step 1.1 shows that $R$ is independent of $Z$.

By [F3], independence from step 2.1 gives the Borel-event factorization required by [F5] for $R$ and $\mathcal G=\sigma(Z)$. The residual is integrable because it is a finite linear combination of square-integrable variables. AC is stated in [A1], so [F5] gives $\mathbb E[R\mid\mathcal G]=\mathbb E[R]=0$; by [F6], this means $\mathbb E[R\mathbf 1_B]=0$ for every $B\in\mathcal G$.

Put $\widehat Y=m_0+\lambda^\top(Z-m)$. This is $\sigma(Z)$-measurable and integrable. For each $B\in\sigma(Z)$, step 3.1 and $Y=\widehat Y+R$ give $\mathbb E[Y\mathbf 1_B]=\mathbb E[\widehat Y\mathbf 1_B]$. Thus [F6] makes $\widehat Y$ a version of $\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(Z)]$, and [F7] gives the asserted almost-sure equality. AC is used only through the Gaussian-law, Gaussian-independence, and conditional-expectation suppliers.

The covariance-based optimality statements on this page use the actual
finite covariance matrix and vector. In particular, the inverse formula for
simple kriging is not asserted when $\Sigma$ is singular.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

derivations.claim: Direct finite summation using [F2] and [F3] gives $\mathbb E[U]=(-1+1)/2=0$ and $\mathbb E[U^2]=1$, so [F4] gives $\operatorname{Var}(U)=1$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(U,U)=1$. Thus the displayed observation covariance has determinant $1-1=0$ and is singular.

The simple predictor is $\lambda_1U+\lambda_2U$ because both known means are zero. Therefore $Y-\lambda^\top Z=(1-\lambda_1-\lambda_2)U$, whose squared expectation is $(1-\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^2\mathbb E[U^2]=(1-\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^2$. It is zero exactly for $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1$, and both $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ give the same random variable $U$.

boundaries.reason: Example fixes Z=(U,U)^T at the two observation sites s1,s2. The singular 2-by-2 covariance and the Verification 2.1 weight-pair calculation concern those two observations, so deleting every observation changes the example.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 identifies all zero-error weights by lambda1+lambda2=1.

citations.quote:
Let $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ be a real random field in the sense of
[[def-random-field-stationarity-covariance-and-variogram]], and suppose the
finite vector of field values considered below is square-integrable. Choose
$n\ge1$ observation sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ and a target site $s_0$. Write
$Z=(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))^\top$, $Y=X(s_0)$,
$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Z)$, $c_0=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)$, and
$v_0=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. A positive-definite matrix $\Sigma$ means
$u^\top\Sigma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$.

If the mean vector $m=\mathbb E Z$ and target mean $m_0=\mathbb E Y$ are
known, a **simple-kriging linear predictor** with weight vector
$\lambda\in\mathbb R^n$ is
$$\widehat Y_{\mathrm{SK}}(\lambda)=m_0+\lambda^\top(Z-m).$$
Its mean-square prediction error is
$\mathbb E[(Y-\widehat Y_{\mathrm{SK}}(\lambda))^2]$.

For an **ordinary-kriging model**, the mean is an unknown common constant
$\theta$: $\mathbb E Z=\theta\mathbf 1_n$ and $\mathbb E Y=\theta$.
The predictor is $\widehat Y_{\mathrm{OK}}(\lambda)=\lambda^\top Z$.
The admissible ordinary weights satisfy $\mathbf 1_n^\top\lambda=1$.

For a **universal-kriging model**, fix a trend map
$p:T\to\mathbb R^q$, where $q\ge1$, and an unrestricted coefficient vector
$\beta\in\mathbb R^q$. Define the finite-site design matrix
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$ by row $i$ equal to $p(s_i)^\top$, and put
$p_0=p(s_0)$. The model means are $\mathbb E Z=P\beta$ and
$\mathbb E Y=p_0^\top\beta$. The predictor is
$\widehat Y_{\mathrm{UK}}(\lambda)=\lambda^\top Z$; its unbiasedness for
every $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ is expressed by $P^\top\lambda=p_0$.
Ordinary kriging is the special case $q=1$, $P=\mathbf 1_n$, and $p_0=1$.

The covariance-based optimality statements on this page use the actual
finite covariance matrix and vector. In particular, the inverse formula for
simple kriging is not asserted when $\Sigma$ is singular.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate $\epsilon_s$, four outcomes have value $1$ and four have value $-1$, so [F2] and [F3] give $\mathbb E[\epsilon_s]=0$ and $\mathbb E[\epsilon_s^2]=1$. For distinct coordinates, each of the four sign pairs occurs twice, so [F4] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_s,\epsilon_t)=0$. Hence the observation-error covariance is $I_2$, which is positive definite.

The two rows of $P$ are linearly independent, but its last two columns are equal, so its rank is two rather than three. For every $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)^\top$, $P^\top\lambda=(\lambda_1+\lambda_2,\lambda_2,\lambda_2)^\top$; its last two coordinates cannot equal the target's $2$ and $4$. Thus no weight vector satisfies $P^\top\lambda=p(s_0)$, so no linear predictor is unbiased for every $\beta$.

Use the notation of [[def-simple-ordinary-and-universal-kriging]]. For
simple kriging, if $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the unique mean-square
minimizing weight vector is $\lambda_{\mathrm{SK}}=\Sigma^{-1}c_0$, and its
mean-square prediction error is
$$v_0-c_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}c_0.$$

For an unknown trend with design matrix $P$ and target vector $p_0$,
$\lambda^\top Z$ is unbiased for every $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ if and only if
$P^\top\lambda=p_0$. Suppose $\Sigma$ is positive definite and $P$ has full
column rank (that is, $Py=0$ implies $y=0$ for $y\in\mathbb R^q$). Then the
unique unbiased mean-square minimizing weights $\lambda\in\mathbb R^n$ and Lagrange
multiplier $\nu\in\mathbb R^q$ solve
$$\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\nu\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_0\\p_0\end{pmatrix}.$$
The augmented matrix is invertible under these hypotheses. The resulting
mean-square prediction error is
$$v_0-\lambda^\top c_0-\nu^\top p_0.$$
For ordinary kriging, take $P=\mathbf 1_n$ and $p_0=1$, giving
$$\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&\mathbf 1_n\\\mathbf 1_n^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\nu\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

derivations.claim: Each $U_i$ has mean zero and second moment one by [F5] and [F6]. For $i\ne j$, each sign pair occurs equally often, so [F7] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,U_j)=0$. Consequently, $\Sigma=I_2$, $c_0=(0,0)^\top$, and $v_0=1$.

When $\theta$ is known, [F3] and step 1.1 give simple weight $\Sigma^{-1}c_0=0$, so the simple minimizing predictor is $\theta$. Its error is $U_0$ and its mean-square error is $\mathbb E[U_0^2]=1$. For the ordinary model, the unbiasedness constraint is $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1$ by [F2].

The ordinary system in [F4] applies because step 1.1 gives $\Sigma=I_2$ and the constant-mean design has full rank. Directly, the ordinary prediction error is $U_0-\lambda_1U_1-\lambda_2U_2$. Expanding its square, all cross terms have expectation zero by step 1.1, so its mean-square error is $1+\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2$. Substituting $\lambda_2=1-\lambda_1$ gives $\frac32+2(\lambda_1-\frac12)^2$, whose unique minimum is $3/2$ at $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1/2$. Since $3/2>1$, ordinary kriging has the larger error in this example.

risk_review.notes: Read all three verification steps and six direct suppliers. Enumerating the eight sign triples gives zero means, unit variances and zero cross-products, hence Sigma=I2,c0=0,v0=1. For every real theta, known-mean simple kriging has weights zero and error U0 of MSE 1. Ordinary unbiasedness for all theta requires lambda1+lambda2=1; on this line the MSE is 1+lambda1^2+lambda2^2=3/2+2(lambda1-1/2)^2. Equal weights uniquely minimize it at 3/2. The constant-mean design has full column rank and Sigma is positive definite; zero c0 is explicitly handled. Empty or one-observation models are outside this fixed two-observation example, and no endpoint restriction on weights or AC is used. Reader/refuter evidence contains no defect here; no general comparison converse is claimed.
